utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, on the basis of the text that I read out, I'd like to question the witness further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you will ask questions. But do you want a number or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that you could record it, but it's early for it to be tendered because the man should come in here to testify live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is simply to mark it for identification rather than tender it. It should not get lost in the record that this trial creates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely that is what we will -- how we will proceed, so we need a MFI number for the last document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be MFI D7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Seselj. You had asked me how much time was left. Well, you had 1 hour and 45 minutes when the hearing started. I don't know how many -- I don't know what you've used up so far, but when we reconvene I will tell you how much time you will have left. But we will not reconvene before 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 5.00 p.m., interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we shall reconvene at 5.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resumed. I'm sorry for this interruption. It was a bit longer than expected. Mr. Seselj, you have 50 minutes left for your cross-examination. I will give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Put your microphone on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreter first said that I had 15 minutes so I was astounded, and then he put himself right and said 50, so that's all right now, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 50.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that's the same according to my calculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, my next question is going to be based on the contents of the following paragraph in the statement of Jovica Stegic. So I'm going to read it out and then I'm going to ask to you either acknowledge or refute what he says, confirm or deny. So listen carefully and I think you have been provided with the text. "The Serbs who came from major Croatian cities did not have the possibility of coming to Serbia and see the real estate for which they exchanged their property, while the Croats, from the Roman Catholic church and the Djakovica bishopsy were given certificates of the Croats with the help of whom they were freely able to go to Croatia and look for property for themselves and then go back to Serbia." And he says: "That is why Mr. Stoparic's claim does not stand that the Croatians were tricked by being shown pictures of houses which looked good, whereas in Serbia, considerably -- houses were in considerably worse condition where waiting for them, whereas in practice the actual state of affairs was quite the reverse?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seem to me that what is being revealed in the publication of this passage is that this person who has provided Mr. Seselj a statement watched the testimony and now is commenting on it and attempting to refute it, and I think that that violates the Trial Chamber's guidelines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is another problem. The person who testified -- who made this testimony will come and will be called, so we'll confront him with it. Mr. Seselj, please finish reading this paragraph and ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have read out the passage and now here comes my question. Mr. Stoparic, do you have knowledge to the effect that the priests of the Roman Catholic church would collect information about the property of Serbs that was abandoned in Croatian and then would inform the Croats before any contracts on the exchange of property were concluded so that in that way they checked the situation out first, what the actual situation was and what the houses concerned were like in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that every individual who wanted to exchange their house with somebody tried to check it out first. That would be logical. Now, whether the Croatian bishopric or Croatian priests did this, well, I never talked to any Croatian priests to know whether they did engage in things like that or not. Can I see the screen again and have this other piece of paper removed from the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you didn't hear that there was mediation by the priests. All right, so that is an answer. So now I am going to read out the following paragraph. There'll be another two or three paragraphs. I'm not going to read the entire text. The owners of the Lasta agency, and you spoke about the Lasta agency at length, were my wife, Mileva Stegic, and myself, we were the owners. The agency for the first seven or eight months was called Juga and after that the name was changed and it became known as Lasta. The agency, throughout the time, until the present day, was officially registered and it functioned in conformity with the law. The Serbian Radical Party had nothing to do with the founding of the agency, nor did it receive any income and remuneration from the work of the agency. I personally, nor the Lasta agency never financed the Serbian Radical Party. Now, what do you think? Is that a -- correct or not, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was a private firm and the gentleman here talks about its establishment and says that the Radical Party had nothing to do with the establishment of the Lasta agency and I never said it did have any connection. I said it was a private firm and I added that I was sure that he was a sponsor like many other businessmen in the town of Sid of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And then the witness said something the interpreter didn't catch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So on the basis of concrete knowledge you say that they were sponsors or you assume that they were probably sponsors, which is it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember now, on one occasion, I was with Mr. Petric, we were visiting this gentleman in his office, and for a time that office was in my street, in Sedni Uli Street. That's where it was located for a time, and I know that Mr. Petric told him about some financial problems, they weren't major financial problems, and I'm quite convinced that he solved the problem for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was that Petric's personal problem or a party problem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petric did not ask for money for himself, for his own personal needs and then to issue a receipt to that effect. You know that there is an annual assembly where the party adopts a budget, everything has to be put down on black and white, how many -- what money came in, what money went out, so I don't believe so. But Petric was a well-to-do man. He had a cafe, he was the proprietor of a cafe, he didn't need to ask for money, so I think that he asked for money for the party and the functioning of the party, I don't think I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Because as in the Serbian Radical Party a final balance is adopted every year at the end of the year, did you see any receipt or certificate to the effect that Jovica Stegic gave some money to the party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember any details like that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stoparic. Let's not dwell on that now. Now, in the next paragraph Jovica Stegic says the following: "The agency functioned on the territory of the whole of Vojvodina and the Croats would contact us from places like Kukujevci, Hrtkovci, Subotica, Zednik and other places. They would contact us freely and themselves state which Croatian town they would like to exchange their properties for. None of the Croats who went to Croatia wanted to go to villages like those from which they had come, which they were leaving but they insisted that they go to large Croatian towns, like Zagreb, Sibenik, Split, Daruvar, Pakrac, Slavonska Pozega, Rijeka and Opatija in which the real estate was much more valuable from real estate in the places they were leaving from, and I maintain contact to this day with many Croats who had exchanged their property through my agency and I guarantee that nobody can find a single one who is dissatisfied or was placed at a disadvantage with the exchange that took place, which, unfortunately, cannot be said of the Serbs. "I personally know of numerous examples of Serbs who even ended up in hospital when they saw what kind of property was waiting for them in Serbia." Now, on the basis of your knowledge and information about the situation in Srem, is what Mr. Stegic says here true or not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe that there were people who attempted in that overall crisis to reap some benefits for themselves. Now, the gentleman says here, and I assume that when he says "most people," that might be 90 per cent, I'm asking why he as a Serb took part at all and mediated when the Serbs always fared worse. How could he do this, morally speaking, if he was a Serb himself?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, I'm asking you questions here. But since you have commented on this, I'm going to actually derive my next question from your comment. Did the Serbs have a choice if an enormous multitude of Serbs had been expelled from Croatia, several hundred thousand of them, in fact, while, at that time in Serbia according to official statistical figures there lived only a hundred thousand Croats in the whole Serbia. Does that mean that the Serbs actually had no choice but were in a situation to accept whatever was offered. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite convicted -- convinced that the refugee Serbs coming to Serbia from Croatia were in a very difficult situation and would be happy to just have a place to sleep. I'm quite convinced of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you now correct your conclusion to the effect that the position of Mr. Stegic was not amoral, seeing that the Serbs were in such a predicament that they had to do something in order to provide a roof over their heads for their families?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not immoral. It is helpful at any rate. Now whether he provided them with a full information, I'm not sure, but I believe that he did. Perhaps I made a mistake on commenting on this, but what I can simply say that some Croats also complained that what they received was not in very good condition. I believe that there was injustice in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question for follow up. To your knowledge were there any Serbs from Croatia who came back to Serbia or in Bosnia-Herzegovina and who, in order to get housing, without any help from anyone just settled in apartments of Croats either by force or because they were empty and just settled in? Have you ever known about this kind situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew of such situations but not in Serbia. They were in the territory of Krajina. The houses were empty and some people moved in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I should like to accentuate once again the question posed by the President of the Bench. So in Serbia you don't know of a single case of Serbs having moved in by force into the house of a Croat?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were attempts after the Oluja.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That is after 1995, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were attempts in certain places, including in Gibarci and Kukujevci but after that very quickly some [indiscernible] special police unit came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And prevented that. Thank you, Mr. Stoparic. Now the next paragraph which I'm going to quote for you, Mr. Stegic says: "It is not true that by 1993 the majority of Croats had left Kukujevci because at that time there was still many of them. The Croats continually exchanged their property and went to -- had been exchanging their property and going to Croatia ever since 1991 and continued to do so until 1996, but the principal reason for that was of an economic nature and not any kind of persecution. Had there been persecution, they would not have been able to peacefully go and look at and choose Serbian estates but would have been expelled in -- comparably faster. There does not exist a single Croat from Srem that has remained without his property or estate. The house of not a single one has been burned or demolished, whereas there are countless examples of exactly that happening in respect of the Serbs." Is this statement correct to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard that any house had been on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Of a Croat.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Serbia, at least not in the general area where I lived and I personally don't believe that anything of that kind could have happened, that is, as far as the burning of houses is concerned or the torching of houses or the destruction in any other way, blowing it up, God forbid, or similar. I never heard of that. The only instance of such a thing was in the village of Lisicic where the Catholic church was blown up. Explosives were planted and it was blown up. That is the only thing that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And this was investigated by the police?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm convinced that they did investigate. How it ended, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, do you know of any case of anyone, of any Croat having been seized of the property of any Croat of his farm facilities or houses having been seized and of any Croat remaining without such property in Serbia, seized property, wrested away property?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, someone just enters his house and settles there and doesn't want -- won't give it to him any back or any of his economic facilities. Well, I have no concrete example of that if anything of that kind happened and I don't know of anyone having threatened anyone else with a rifle and expelling them from their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you agree with my contention that literally not a single Croat in Serbia, especially not in Vojvodina remained without his property, without his real estate, immovable property?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, sooner or later they managed to either exchange or sell that property.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see. Well, I shall quote another portion of this document for you. Mr. Stegic says: "It is an absolute lie that I hosted a lunch after the visit of Dr. Vojislav Seselj to Kukujevci in 1993. It is easy to prove that Vojislav Seselj visited Kukujevci. It was first written the 13th of May here and then corrected into the 15th of May, 1993 at a time when I not only was not in Kukujevci but was not in Serbia either. To prove this I attached this statement a photostatic copy of my military service booklet which demonstrates that in the period from the 4th of March 1993 to 18th of August 1993 I was in the army of the republic of the Serb Krajina in the military garrison 9039, Knin."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to clarify. Are we speaking about MFI D7? Because the copy I have does not have a military booklet attached to it as stated by Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What are you referring to, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You saw the military booklet before this. It has already been tendered as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it the military booklet of this witness here in the courtroom or another one -- of the other one? Because we have two military booklets, the one of the witness and there's another military booklet, Mr. Stegic's military booklet. So which one are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not interested in Mr. Stoparic's military booklet. We are now talking about this document which I have already shown to Mr. Stoparic and which has been tendered into the file. That is the Jovica Stegic's military booklet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is the one. Please show it to Mrs. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number D6.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: -- the document I was given for D7 is a three-page document and there's nothing to indicate that the person who signed this document included this military booklet with it. They were presented as separate pieces of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. These are two separate documents. So this -- the military booklet is D6.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not written here that a military booklet is a component part of the statement, but it is attached to this statement, enclosed to it. That is what the statement says. But I shall now like to move on to a new set of questions because I want to make the best of the remaining time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, you are a literate person, are you not, I suppose that you have read a book of mine, that you have at least had one in your hands?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read the paper Velika Srbija and many times the paper contained excerpts from your books and I have seen your books and I have held them in the offices of the Serbian Radical Party, but I never took one home and read it in extenso.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you ever seen or held in your hands this book?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And would you be so kind as to pass it to Mr. Stoparic.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have an opportunity to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, is this a book that you already disclosed to Prosecution or is this a book that Prosecution has never had in its hands?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not disclosed it. I have disclosed to the OTP 80 of my books in 2003 but not this one. Whether the Prosecutor has had a chance to see it, I don't know. But I'm going to ask just one question of Mr. Stoparic once he has seen the book.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can I ask Mr. Seselj to please read the title of the book into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, could you please read the title of this book.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The title of this book is

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, have you ever seen that book?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. I don't know your language, but in French I heard "and the (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Judge, sir. It does have --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: So we are talking about a negative trait of character which has nothing to do with conventional classical prostitution but it is a very frequent occurrence in public life. This is the most graphic explanation of this term.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And ask a question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Judge, how the Bench can censor the titles of my books. This book could have been incriminatory material, you could have put me on trial for this book and without having the title of that book in the transcript this is not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, just a minute. You come from a country which is a civil law country just like mine, and you know that in civil law there can be prosecution for libel. A book may very well infringe on somebody's dignity, and so there can always be a civil lawsuit, maybe even a criminal lawsuit. This is why this Chamber with three Judges cannot let this slide, cannot accept this. This is a libelous title and it could very well jeopardise somebody's dignity, and this is why the Chamber believes that this word should be redacted. That's all. But ask your question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I protest on that account, because of the title of this book and neither the Bench nor the witness nor the Prosecution can be held accountable or held to account. Only I myself can be held to account because of the title of this book if Natasa Kandic sues me before the competent Serbian Court and the competent court is the court where these -- of the place in which this book was published. The book came out some time ago. It was promoted in 30 days -- cities of Serbia. It was in fact also disclosed to Natasa Kandic, put under her very nose in a TV show, a TV duo with my advisor Aleksandar Vucic and she has not filed any charges against me and you are now telling me this. I'm not going to shun any responsibility if I am indeed sued for it by Natasa Kandic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we are not involved in censorship, but we believe that there is a word that could jeopardise this lady that we don't know and could infringe on her rights even if this book is well known in your country and so forth. This Tribunal cannot be the media by which this word is being propagated, a word that could very well be found libelous in the different courts. It would be exactly the same if someone came here before us and insulted you similarly. We would also believe that a redaction is required. You know, it goes both ways. Now, please come to the substance, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I'm going to move on to my next question. If you have redacted the title of my book, then I would like to move on to my next question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, in Serbia, was any kind of case brought against you for tortuous liability?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you could have been punished for a minor infraction and also there have been a halt in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many such proceedings were brought against you? Do you remember, misdemeanours and other such offences?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice. It was an accident that had something to do with a car, so it was a traffic accident. And once, I was punished for possessing a weapon. However, this was probation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There is no probation for misdemeanours.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just telling what it was that I remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to inform you then if you don't know. My legal advisors looked at the records of the municipal court in Sid, so we're just talking about Sid, they received information on the 22nd of January this year, that so far you were 17 times --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, hold on a minute. You're a legal expert and I'm sure that in your country there must be misdemeanours which can be just lifted or were no longer on criminal records, and in that case you cannot mention convictions where there was an amnesty or -- so if you're talking about a misdemeanour, an offense that is in this category in a legal sense, you're not allowed to mention these, since-- if they have benefitted from amnesty. I don't know which one you're referring to, but sometimes there are laws that make it possible to just erase a criminal record if they're just misdemeanours on this criminal record, and I think you need to know about this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, crimes, after a while, are also erased from records but not misdemeanours. Misdemeanours are something that administrative agencies are in charge of, not the judiciary. A misdemeanours court is not a classical court but it is a court under the jurisdiction of the ministry of the interior, that is to say of an administrative agency, and that is not deleted from records.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So far, Mr. Stoparic, misdemeanour proceedings were brought against you 17 times. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm going to show you the document. Most of these misdemeanours have to do with the law on public peace and order, some are related to traffic, some proceedings were initiated at the request of the power company and so on. Would you look at these records and would you tell us what it is that is not true if you think there is something here that is untrue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may take a moment to look at this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have a question. In your country can you ask administration to deliver a document that would list all of the misdemeanours that a person may have committed?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not every citizen can do that. However, in accordance with the Law on Cooperation between Yugoslavia, or rather now Serbia, with The Hague Tribunal, state organs are in principle duty-bound to make available to my legal advisors all accessible information, all information that I could use for my Defence. Inter alia they gave me almost my complete dossier from the secret police, from the state security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document doesn't bear any signature or any seal. It is not what I would recognise as an official court record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... Look at it. Mr. Seselj, this document was faxed; that's obvious. It has no signature. It just lists a number of offences that are dated. But why is there no signature or seal?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not an official document that I would admit into evidence. Quite simply, this is an excerpt from computer records and it contains important information including the case numbers, the cases against Mr. Stoparic. And if you wish, you can officially ask the courts to submit the documents for you and then have that admitted into evidence. I wanted to show this to Mr. Stoparic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: This appears to be an improper attempt at impeachment. The witness was asked about a record of misdemeanours, he denied it, and now he is being presented with a list of information that is not an official document and doesn't contain information about the nature of the offence. All of the dates even seem to be even quite historical, quite attenuated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness might be in a position to rebut this or confirm it. Just show him the document. Look at it, Mr. Stoparic, look at the document, see what's in it. What do you think of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that I was a very naughty boy in my municipality when I was a young man. That's what this document seems to suggest. I don't remember this many fines or penalties. I never said that I was a saint. These are just misdemeanours when I was young.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For instance, which is the first offence? Can you read it out, the first one. Just the first one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was punished for the misdemeanour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please read slower. Interpreter's note, it is too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I had a quarrel with someone, maybe I even had a fight physically with someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is just misdemeanours. There is no crime as such.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a misdemeanour that involves a fine, according to law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: There was no English interpretation of what the witness was reading because of the speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, please read the first part again, what is in it, because the Prosecutor could not hear it in her language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I thought that I am a witness in this courtroom, not that I would have to bring you a birth certificate. Maybe I was a naughty boy even then but I'm going to read it. He was punished for the misdemeanour from paragraph 3, item 3, from the law on misdemeanours and the date is the 25th of July, 1990 and he was fined.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, what is the last misdemeanour under number 17?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not going to read it at all. It's my personal matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It cannot be personal. I'm checking your credibility here. You have to answer.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't want to go into closed session. I am checking your credibility before the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I don't know what is under number 17. Is it something that you do not want to make public? Are you asking for private session? The Trial Chamber will see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll read it. I'll read it. You don't have to go into closed session. Shall I? Proceedings were instituted for a misdemeanour from the field of traffic but the proceedings were halted due to a statute of limitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stopped in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, how many times were criminal charges brought against you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was punished for possessing a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many times were criminal charges brought against you, that's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, there are three judgments, final judgments, due to crimes you committed. Listen to me carefully. The first one of the municipal court from Sid dated the 12th of June, 1996 for petty theft, article 73/1 of the criminal law of Serbia, you were fined. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Oh. In 1996, you do not remember. Then the second time the municipal court in Sid, on the 27th of October, 1997, in accordance with Article 195 of the criminal law of Serbia, spent 30 days in prison. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is Article 195? What is this? You have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's an Article of the law, 195/1. Is it correct that you were sentenced to 30 days in prison or not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was detained once, because I was somewhere and I did not report before the court and it precisely had to do with possession of weapons and it ended with this punishment that I referred to already, but I don't think it was 30 days that was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were sentenced by a district court in Sremska Mitrovica. That is K19/95 on the 9th of May, 1997 in accordance with the law on weapons and ammunition. You were sentenced to six months in prison, one year suspended. So these are two different laws. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Oh, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, through official channels you can receive a complete report on the criminal charges brought against Mr. Stoparic so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I do not challenge the fact that there have been offences in spite of the fact that the witness says that he doesn't remember some of them. There are others he admits. Which is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I challenge the credibility of this witness I just want to make it known to you that criminal charges were brought against him several times and many times he was tried for misdemeanours. I think that's important for the credibility of a witness, and you can think whatever you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, were you arrested in Beli Manistir as well and were you held there in prison for 15 days?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you are saying, Seselj, is all one particular deed. It has to do with this weapon thing that I referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before you even mentioned crimes, I said that I was given a suspended sentence for possession of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, these were large quantities of weapons, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were large quantities of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that's what I wanted you to confirm. It is because of large quantities of weapons the criminal charges were brought against you. I have a list of these weapons here. If necessary, I can present it. If not, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not necessary. It's an adequate punishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it's not that the punishment was very severe at that time but they did take away these weapons, right, and it was an entire arsenal. I have all the list of all these weapons here. Do you want to have a look or are you not interested?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I memorized it. I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Oh, I see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Move on to something else, Mr. Seselj. The witness does not challenge the fact that he had weapons in his possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to know this of the witness. What is the year in which this happened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, those weapons. In which year did you have them, 1994, 1995, 1996, 1997? To your recollection, which year was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is this court and this Trial Chamber that looked into this problem of weapons. I mean, you're not asking me now to explain to you how come all these weapons happened to be on me and where all these weapons came from. Now, what year this was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're interested in the year. The year is the thing. Is it straight after the war or a long time after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In some territories the war was still on. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: From 1994 onwards. Let me help you. First of all it was in 1994 when you tried to bring in one -- two automatic rifles, one --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speaker will have to read slower. The interpreter cannot keep up.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not getting any interpretation. Mr. Seselj needs to perhaps read much, much slower.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat it slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: For example, the first criminal report was filed in 1994, on the 15th of March. You were brought into custody and handed over to the judge of the municipal court in Sid because you entered the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at -- in Sid in a 1300 Lada that did not have registration plates that was owned by a person from Oriolik --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the following weapons were found on you: Two automatic rifles one hunting carbine, one military carbine with a sniper, one Magnum revolver, one pistol of the Srbinje [phoen] Zastava make, one hand-grenade. Roughly all the other crimes relate to that too. I really don't have to read all of this out, do I. Mostly it was weapons, all of it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I was given a suspended sentence for possession of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, sir. For your information, Mr. Seselj, you have 20 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm bringing it to an end, Judge. I am hurrying as much as I can, but I'm speaking slower because of the interpreters. Maybe you've noticed. One more thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm making it known to you that I received a document from this Office of the Prosecutor that shows that the state security service also kept you under surveillance because you brought large quantities of weapons from the front line and stored them in your own apartment. The number given to it by the OTP is 06076918 and the date is the 28th of September, 1993. That was an indicator to me to continue this search. Had the Prosecutor not given me this, I wouldn't have been looking, but that's the kind of man I am. What can I say?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Now the speakers are overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not angry at you. You're a very pleasant witness as far as I'm concerned?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must understand that at that time many people had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. You explained to us here that when Miro Vujevic were arrested, and Stanko Vujanovic, that Kameni came, Kinez and Ceca had a meeting in your presence in order to dovetail their statements expecting to be detained themselves. Is that the truth?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was after Miroljub Vujanovic and -- or rather, Milo Vujevic and Stanko Vujanovic were arrested?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them had certainly been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now I have a sorry piece of news for you. I received a letter -- a glad piece of news for you from Ceca which I received from the prison. Would you like to read the letter? It was faxed to me through the mediation of my legal advisors. Would you read it out loud, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, could you inform the Trial Chamber who is the detainee who sent you a letter?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is Ceca, no, I don't know his first and last name but anyway, Mr. Stoparic spoke about him at length. He was one of the combatants and officers in Leva Supoderica, the Leva Supoderica Detachment, in fact, and he was arrested together with Kameni and Kinez because -- on suspicion that they had taken part in Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're going to give the document --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a handwritten letter. There's no indication that it is under oath and it again is referring to criticisms of the testimony by somebody outside the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to show it to him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll provide some information.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can we please have it marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be MFI D8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Would you read it out loud, please, the letter so that we can hear it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's improper impeachment. If there is some information or question that Mr. Seselj would like to put the witness, he can ask a question. But it is not appropriate to have letters faxed into the courtroom from some third party and then republished as a means of cross-examination. If there is a fact that Mr. Seselj wants to controvert, he should ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, the Vukovar case was, in part, tried here. In our indictment, we also have to settle this matter, and we know that there was a trial in Serbia on these same facts. So there's quite a blend, a mix, and we do not have all the facts. It appears that one of the participants who is detained has sent a letter to Mr. Seselj - I don't know what for, for what purpose - but I see that from what the accused said, the sender of this letter was part of the unit in which Mr. Stoparic had a position. The witness knows this person, the one who seems to have written this letter. I don't know personally what is in the letter. So, Witness, you have read the letter. Is there any problem reading it, or don't you want to read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll read it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first part is illegible. The letters are too small. If Mr. Seselj agrees I can begin with the following words: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, have a go and try and read it all out. Do you want me to lend you my glasses? Do have a go.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Suggest that we put it on the ELMO because then the interpreters can see it, and if they can read it, perhaps they can assist -- can interpret what Mr. Stoparic is reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is going to be put on the ELMO. There it is. Please read out, Mr. Stoparic, whatever you can read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stoparic, on the 15th of January --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it, I found where we're showing it. Continue, please. Apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Stoparic on the 15th of January, 2008 at an interview in The Hague said roughly the following: That he and Kameni, because they heard that Miroljub and Stanko had been arrested, came to Sremska Mitrovica to see me and then we all went to Ruma to Kinez in order to reach an agreement. As the lawyer told us to go back home and forget everything, forget about it. I don't know if you can let Vojo know. I think that means you. I consider it important that you know the following: I was arrested on the 21st of January, 2003, that is to say in January, and Stanko and Miroljub, in Sabljak in March or April of 2003. This is proof and evidence that Stoparic is lying because Kameni -- he could not have come with Kameni to see me because at the time I was in detention at the moment when Stanko and Miroljub were arrested. Greetings, Ceca."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your question, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, you didn't know that Ceca had been arrested before Miroljub Vujevic and Stanko Vujanovic, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sitting in a catering establishment with Ceca and talking about the possible arrest and taking into custody with respect to Ovcara and the beginning of the trial in Serbia. Now what Ceca wrote here, the date of his arrest and when one of the others whether, Miroljub or Stanko were arrested, I don't know whether they were arrested there. I except Vojvoda Kameni to send a letter and he is much more honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, I came here on the 24th of February, 2003. And already at that time, as far as I remember, they hadn't been arrested, either Stanko Vujanovic or Miroljub Vujevic. It was after Zoran Djindjic's killing in the operation there, but obviously you don't remember that. All right, Mr. Stoparic. And they slipped that in for you to sign too and now you have nowhere to go.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much more time do I have, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you still have ten minutes, but we're going to be told this by the court deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'll end on time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, you stated here that in a western country -- you live in a western country now and that you earn your living through your firm. You said that you established a firm and that that provides a livelihood for you. However, when you left Serbia you had no money at all. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What money do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I mean more than 1.000 or 2.000 Euros, for example. You had no employment, you were wounded, you were undergoing rehabilitation, you couldn't earn any serious money, could you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I lived like many others in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I agree. I asked your family, too, your brothers live in a very modest way, your father was an honest and decent man, he was never very rich. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 80 per cent in my town lived that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Your younger brother is quite ill and he finds it difficult to meet ends meet and your older brother couldn't help you too much. He could offer you hospitality, you had your meals with him, gave you some money to buy something, but he couldn't actually provide for your livelihood. He didn't have enough money to cater to all your needs. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, sir, that we're from Srem and that we all have our pigs and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, you can't live from just one pig.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you said you had investigated my family, and if you had done that you would have seen that he has at least 40 pigs now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How much -- how many did he have when you left and emigrated?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe more than 40 pigs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And how much revenue can 40 pigs provided?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his wife works and his younger brother works.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But there is not too much money to throw around?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in Serbia nobody has that much money that they can throw it around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Anyway, you came here. You lived on 900 Euros in some western country. You came you to the Tribunal first and they sent you on further. They gave you shelter somewhere. I'm not going to mention the country. And you had 900 Euros a month, that's what you said yourself. And then you opened your own company. Where did you get the money, the initial capital to open a company of your own?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seselj, I married in the meantime. My wife does not come from the former Yugoslavia. She is employed. She works too. I made some money and managed to save some money too, and there's a building where it says "bank." And then you set out your problem in that building. You ask them how much money they can give you and they give you loans to set up your firm and they place you on stand-by for tax purposes for half a year and for the repayment of your loan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I understand that, but banks usually ask for somebody's guarantee. Who guaranteed for you, who was the guarantor?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had my -- a guarantee from my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did she have any real estate, any property to back up this guarantee.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the basis of that, you were given a loan and you managed to open up your -- set up your firm. I'm just asking. I don't want to upset you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. It appears to be ranging too far afield into the witness's private affairs. It does not seem to have any bearing on the witness's credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not the point. You know as well as I do, Ms. Dahl, that in many writings the accused said that some witnesses may have received money from the Prosecution. This is what he is trying to establish or check. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, rather than fishing into Mr. Stoparic's private financial affairs, he can ask the witness directly if he received funds from the Prosecution instead of going into his banking relationship and his wife's finances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it would be quicker if you went straight to the crux of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, when did you buy a car?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eight months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what car did you buy?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Chrysler Voyager.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How much did it cost?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What's the cost of that car?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I pay a repayment of 150 Euros a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Which car did you have before that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have a car, but before that I had to get a driver's licence, learn the language and you need a driving licence in every country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And which car did you have before you emigrated?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a time I went out with a girl, or, rather I helped her in the work of her cafe and I used her car but I didn't have my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't purchase a car before that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Among other things, you said that as a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party, you went to war in the area of Livno, in 1992, the first half of 1992, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the spring.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What month roughly would you say?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was still quite cold.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it February, March?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Anyway, you went to Bosansko Grahovo and the front towards Livno, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We came from Bihac airport and then from Bihac we were transported to Knin and from Knin to Bosansko Grahovo Strmica and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm now going to tell you what my information about that is and then I'll ask for your comments. I never heard that volunteers of Serbian Radical Party went to war around Bosansko Grahovo and the front towards Livno, so I checked this out. In the archives of the party there is no information about that. I asked the chief of the war staff, Ljubisa Petkovic, and his deputies Zolo and Drazilovic and they confirmed that the Serbian Radical Party never had its volunteers in that particular area. So who's right here, all of us or you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All your sources are your own. They're your own sources. I could not - and you know this. This was immediately after the fall of Kupres. A normal corridor had not been established yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When did Kupres fall, Mr. Stoparic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was before the fall of Kupres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when did Kupres fall?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When did Kupres fall?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army and a colonel made his name there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, you said here that Ratko Mladic came to visit the troops, right, and that General Ratko Mladic proposed that you do not leave any prisoners. What did he say?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say that. He said I'm not interested in pets but in Livno, take care of the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that mean that you could kill everybody, including pets and if you enter Livno, you should take care of the civilians? Have I interpreted that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, General Ratko Mladic became the commander of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska only on the 12th of May, 1992. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. I don't know the exact date when he became the commander of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I do.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is excellent. But before he became commander of Republika Srpska army, he probably had the rank of general or colonel. He was still Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But how come he was in that area?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know -- I'm sure you know that before he became commander of the army of Republika Srpska that he was the commander in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was the deputy to General Vukovic in the Knin Corps. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the post he held but in the Knin Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So how come he was at the front towards Livno?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you either don't want to know or perhaps you don't really know where Bosansko Grahovo is situated and where the sector below Mount Dinavar is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I know that full well. I was there myself but in later years.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very close to the border with the Knin-Krajina area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What you mean to say is that the Knin Corps had control of that area, is that it? It does border on Knin-Krajina but the Knin Corps did not hold the lines facing Livno between Bosansko Grahovo and Livno? Never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, for your information, you have five more minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There existed two Krajina corps, the 1st Krajina Corps and the 2nd Krajina Corps. Are you clear on that? They were made from the Banja Luka and the Bihac Corps within the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. Are you clear on that? When the Republika Srpska was proclaimed, they were renamed the 1st and the 2nd Krajina Corps. Do you know that at all?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There existed the 1st Krajina Corps and probably there existed the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They definitely did, I can guarantee that to you as a Chetnik duke.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no doubt that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How come the Knin Corps was between Bosansko Grahovo and Livno? Whenever I went to Knin I went via Bosansko Grahovo. I know the route but I know that the Knin Corps was never there.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you saying that there was no concerted action between these two armies?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There was concerted action but General Ratko Mladic could not have shown up there.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what you say, what you claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I claim that it is so and I claim another thing and I will wait for -- to hear your position on that. And that is that I claim that the OTP is preparing you primarily as a false witness in a possible trial of Ratko Mladic if they happened by some unfortunate circumstance to lay their hands on him.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But I also contend that they were preparing you for a false witness in Slobodan Milosevic's trial in the additional Prosecution case after the Defence case had terminated. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't have to claim that. That was so, but the late Judge May refused me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And I'm also claiming that the OTP is preparing you as a false witness in the cases against Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, were you to testify in Slobodan Milosevic's trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as I know, I was scheduled. I was supposed to feature in some additional part of the case, as Mr. Seselj said, but I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Because Mr. Milosevic died before the completion of the Defence case, and you would have actually taken the stand had he not died?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, you gave a statement to the OTP of the Tribunal also because you met the legal advisors of Slobodan Milosevic in a cafe when -- at the time when you were being prepared to take the stand?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not a statement. I just informed them of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But I got the statement. I have received the statement. It is a statement. You informed them and they took a statement from you immediately thereafter, did they not, and you described it, they saw you, they looked at you in the cafe and you immediately got frightened that there was some danger actually threatening you coming from them. Did you not?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Can we ask Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Document and if it is a statement that he's examining the witness on that the witness be given a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the document you have, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking for it right now, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have to -- you will have to finish soon because you have no more time. But you can put this question once you find the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would end with this. This is document which is not marked and the date of the talk is the 26th of February, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Interview conducted by Paolo Pastore Stocchi, if I read it correctly, and General Saxton. See if I pronounced the name correctly. Statement has some five pages. You were escorted by policemen from Belgrade on -- on the plane. In front of you these policemen said good-bye to Milosevic's legal advisors and then in an Italian restaurant, the La Bruschetta Italian restaurant in The Hague in the van der Goesstraat street 9 and near the hotel where you are staying. That is the hotel where all the witnesses stay who are being prepared to testify, and indeed my own advisors also stay there. So you entered this place and you saw some of Milosevic's advisors there and that scared you so much that you had to immediately give a statement to the OTP. There was this junior lawyer who noticed me. He stared at me and he certainly must have recognised me. He took out his phone, and he actually talked to somebody and according -- that is in paragraph 13. He looked at me and Tapuskovic stared at me, and I was under the impression that they were talking about me. I immediately paid my bill and went to sleep. That's your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, the statement is available in available in e-court under Document Number 65 ter 07036. So the witness can have an opportunity to review what he is apparently being examined on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, put the question to the witness since he remembers the statement, he must have signed it. So put the question to the witness regarding that document, and you will then end your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did this scare you, Mr. Stoparic, when you saw Milosevic's legal advisors and assumed that they were talking about you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now it would not frighten me. At that time I had this feeling, it was not actually fear, but I was apprehensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So that particular year you associated that with the procrastination of the issuance of your passport in Serbia and the threats being levelled at your family at the time, and that is why you did not feel secure; and you actually were -- loathed to go back to Serbia. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seselj, I was brought to The Hague escorted by the police as a protected person of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I should like to say one thing, Mr. Stoparic. In Serbia you were never seriously endangered, but you just made people believe that you were endangered by statements of this kind in similar statements in order to actually elicit from the OTP of the Tribunal as a valuable witness of theirs to be placed in a western country, to be financially provided for, and to get the working permit, a residence permits, something that thousands, hundreds of thousands of people hailing our poor parts would actually covered. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you except to me to say that it is right, or that it is not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I expect to you say that it is right, but I'm not sure that you will actually fulfil my exceptions right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, your time is up. Very well, Ms. Dahl do you have any re-direct questions in re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to remind you that questions in re-direct are always linked or they stem from the questions that were put during the cross-examination; so it is better to say during the cross-examination Mr. Seselj asked you this question you answered in this way and I would like to clarify this and this. Very well. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Stoparic, Mr. Seselj asked about your attendance at campaign rallies and your exposure to his ideas before you volunteered to go to the front lines. Before you volunteers in 1991, how did you learn of Mr. Seselj's political ideas?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were publicly accessible to all.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you hear him giving television interviews?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How about on the radio?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I listened to him on the radio also, but later when he was on a local radio in my city, and I don't exactly remember whether I had also heard him on Belgrade radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you read any news reports about his ideas?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the programme was not in the usually ordinary daily papers but Seselj's statements were often quoted as were those of other politicians.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You mentioned today in cross-examination about a publication called Velika Srbija. Can you tell me what that is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a magazine, the magazine, issued by the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Could you encapsulate for me the political ideas that Mr. Seselj was advocating concerning Serbs and Serbia during the war?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political ideas advocated by Mr. Seselj and his party are known to all. One need not be a participant in the war to say something or know to something at least partially about it. Greater Serbia that was the objective and of course the political struggle in order to assume power, that was the objective. That is what a political after all is for. But within the greater framework of Greater Serbia, there are many other things that can be talked about. I'm just saying this in global terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Mr. Seselj's political ideas about Greater Serbia have some influence in your decision to volunteer?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it did actually awake some patriotism in me. Of course, I wanted Serbia to be big, to be rich, to be respected and the bigger country it is status, the more respected it is; that is quite clear. At that time, I did see a logical foundation to it. There were indeed so many Serbs and many Serbs living in all those areas that he mentioned. That is a historical fact. I cannot say that I personally did not want a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday during the war in Herzegovina you saw groups of people in the street calling themselves Seselj's Men.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't have to just confine ourselves to Herzegovina. Everywhere in Serbia or elsewhere, you could see people for instance in the street singing a song extolling Seselj or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many people, members of the army of the Republika Srpska also did the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: From what you say of their songs or expressions, did they seem to be in agreement with the idea of achieving a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note could the witness please take his hand off his mouth and speak in the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were already at war and of course they concurred in the idea that his house, their house should remain part of Serbia or Yugoslavia. I don't see why they should agree to the idea of a Greater Serbia or, if nothing else for it to be called Yugoslavia and for Croatia and these others to secede but only within the ethnic Croats or ethnic Muslims boundaries. Every Serb in other words wanted his city, his village to be either in Serbia or in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And yesterday you discussed with Mr. Seselj the areas in which you served in military combat during the war in Croatia and the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Your objective in this military service was to take strategic control of -- of locations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not strategic control, absolute control. When we take a terrain and inhabit a place we put in an attack in order to gain absolute control of it; or perhaps if it was a Serbian village that needed liberating that that was the objective.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, in the areas that were outside of Serbia, were the locations strategically related to unifying places of Serb populations?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not quite sure I understand strategic places. There were strategic objectives for instance at one of time was the penetration of the corridor, because without the corridor the Serbs in the Knin Krajina would have no prospects at all. They would be actually at the mercy of the Croatian MUP and would soon have been extinguished; so we did have strategic objectives in our struggle, although I'm not a member of the Main Staff to be aware of each individual and every single strategic objective; but it was quite logical that they were in existence. It was the strategic objective we had one Serbian enclave and another and no continental link between them to ensure that link. That was a strategic objective, which was only logical.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me see if I understand your testimony correctly. When you would take control of a location, that would include expelling or cleansing the area of the enemy?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we as Serbian soldiers took a village, it went without saying that we would meet with the resistance of the enemy forces. If we were gaining the upper hand, they would flee, so that was the cleansing that was certainly be supposed to take place of every enemy soldier that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And yesterday in your examination by Mr. Seselj you discussed the need to evacuate the civilians from these locations that you were taking control of.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must ask me more specifically. I do remember being

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presiding Judge asked me a few questions. Evacuation is a normal thing we also attack -- evacuate our own civilians. It is not logical to leave them within the range of artillery or shelling or rifle bullets of the other side of the enemy side, and the other side did the same. The enemy side did the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I think that this came in the context of the Presiding Judge's questions about artillery fire and moving civilians out of the villages that were being taken over.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was not us that were removing the civilian population. It was their army that was actually withdrawing the civilians from the area concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was in response to being shelled with artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is simply a precautionary measures. Artillery weapons is not always precise. They can overshoot their targets.
